title: Character Strengths, Integrity, and My Three-Year-Old
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart opens with rehearsing gratitude with his three-year-old and realizing he owed a thank-you note he had neglected for months, then turns the moment into an argument about teaching character strengths. He contends that teachers who post strengths like zest, gratitude, grit and social intelligence must be working on them personally, since experiential knowledge underwrites teacher credibility. Because this is impossible to do perfectly, hypocrisy is inevitable, and he borrows Carol Dweck's point about growth mindset to argue that consistency is a journey rather than a proclamation. He then recovers the etymological sense of integrity as wholeness: an integrated life with fewer seams between public and private selves, including how teachers talk about students and colleagues. Such integration, he argues, frees mental energy that self-deception and multiple selves consume. He concludes, with David Brooks, that such eulogy virtues take a lifetime to refine.
points: Stuart argues that teachers should only teach the character strengths they are actively working on themselves, because experience drives credibility.
Hypocrisy is inevitable in this work, and the right response is to treat consistency as a journey rather than claim an identity of having arrived.
He reclaims integrity in its root sense of wholeness, aiming for a life with fewer seams between how one acts with students, family, church and colleagues.
Talking about students and colleagues in private as one never would in public costs not only morally but in performance, by draining mental energy.
Following David Brooks, he distinguishes resume virtues on the classroom wall from eulogy virtues that take a lifetime to refine.
quotes: As Laura's father, my desire is that gratitude be well-developed in her, both externally (in the habit of saying “thank you”) and internally (in the habit of focusing on all she has versus all she doesn't). I want these things for Laura not because I look like a good dad when she says “Thank you,” but because external gratitude will make her a blessing to others and internal gratitude is a great source of motivation. In short, I want Laura to live a flourishing life, and gratitude is one of the surest means toward that.

If you're going to teach character strengths well, you've got to have experiential knowledge about what you're talking about. This lends to your teacher credibility, which John Hattie's “Visible Learning” meta-analysis has found to be a significant factor in student outcomes (effect size .90, as found in Visible Learning for Teachers).
Just as growth mindset is a journey, so, too, is the consistent life, the life devoid of hypocrisy, the life where the character strengths we teach are the ones we master daily.

When I say I want to live an integrated life — a life of integrity — it certainly means that I hope to be honest and morally upright, but even more than that it means that I want to iron out the seams in my life. I want there to be less of a jarring sensation when I see a student in the local grocery store while I'm with my wife and children, or when my friends from church see me interact with my relatives or my colleagues. In short, I want to be like an integer in math class, a “whole number”; I want to be consistent.

Or let me bring it to a place that every teacher can relate to: I want the conversations I have about students and colleagues and bosses to be the kinds of conversations I wouldn't be humiliated to have broadcasted for the world to see. I know my own tendency to speak in private like I never would in public — and that bothers me not just from the obvious moral standpoint, but also from the performance standpoint. And my goal with this paragraph is to produce introspection, not guilt.

What mental energies do I unconsciously spend keeping my stories straight and my multiple selves correctly hidden or displayed? How much more force might we bring to bear on problems in our classrooms or our homes if we weren't undermining the people we're working to become, the legacies we're hoping to leave, with small, self-deceiving excuses (“Well, I'll just neglect this one thank you note a bit longer,” or, “I'm just joking around with my friends — it's harmless.”)

This is because they spend huge swaths of their academic lives engaged in a dizzying array of tasks that target a mind-numbing myriad of standards. I think this creates a school day that is mildly entertaining, depending on the teacher, but ultimately senseless. This experience, I would argue, is so dis-integrated that it functionally aids in the disintegration of our students' minds.
